title: Teachers Try to Squeeze in More Reading Time
author: Ava Gordon
summary: This reported piece by Ava Gordon, a journalism student working as Holly Korbey's reporting intern, asks whether students get enough time with real text. Interviews with elementary teachers show them using Teach Like a Champion's FASE group reading, extending reading routines into science and social studies, and adopting a vocabulary-focused Word Mapping curriculum, while often working around mandated curricula that leave little room for reading. Researchers behind the SRI Bridging the Divide report add that science of reading policies may be crowding out real reading, since over half the classrooms they studied in urban districts rarely moved beyond individual words. They recommend weaving vocabulary and fluency into phonics lessons so word recognition and language comprehension are practised together. Teachers also name homework, phones, and student motivation as obstacles, and Gordon admits her own reading has given way to TikTok. No single method wins; the teachers advise testing approaches in their own classrooms. A survey of Bell Ringer readers is cited but is likely skewed toward more reading than average.
points: Several teachers say reading time is squeezed by mandated curricula and a crowded school day, so they extend reading routines into science and social studies.
FASE group reading gives the teacher control over who reads next, keeps students attentive, and lets the teacher target specific skills.

The SRI researchers worry that phonics-heavy implementation of science of reading laws leaves too little time for connected text, and propose a bridging process that links word recognition to comprehension.
A structured vocabulary curriculum raised fluency and test confidence for one teacher, who stopped reading texts aloud to students as a result.

Teachers pair test-score tactics with efforts to build a love of reading, such as strong classroom libraries and conversation about books, because students who like reading will read more outside school.
quotes: After seeing the shift in my students’ fluency last year, I’m no longer going to read any text to them,” Dylla said. Students are going to read it themselves.

Dylla’s realization highlights an important question, especially now with science of reading laws focusing so much on early phonics—educators might be paying more attention to whether students can read the words, but what about the goal: the quantity of real reading?

Overall, I learned that more time spent reading makes better readers, according to the teachers I talked to, but it’s hard to make the time with a curriculum that is packed with content teachers are required to teach.

Maybe somewhat ironically, science of reading laws and policies, with their increased focus on phonics, might be cutting into student reading time. Researchers for the SRI Bridging the Divide study found many classrooms focus too much on phonics rather than “real reading.” More than half of classrooms in the urban districts they studied rarely moved beyond reading individual words.
